notes.meaning: The prophet calls on the northern mountains of Lebanon to throw open their gates as judgment approaches like a roaring fire. In ancient times, foreign armies often invaded the land by marching through these northern mountain passes and cutting down the prized cedar forests. Many early teachers also saw Lebanon as a symbol for the temple in Jerusalem, which was built with these magnificent cedar beams.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators frequently understand Lebanon as a direct title for the temple in Jerusalem, noting early Jewish records that its heavy doors swung open on their own before the Roman destruction.

notes.meaning: When the towering cedars fall, the smaller cypress trees and mighty oaks are told to wail because their turn has come. In the language of prophecy, these trees represent different ranks of people in the nation. If the great and powerful leaders cannot withstand the coming storm, the common people have no hope of escaping.

The devastation sweeps down to the lush Jordan valley, ruining the rich pastures where flocks once grazed. The rulers wail because their glory and wealth have been stripped away. Even the young lions roar in distress because the dense thickets where they once hunted have been wiped out.

God commands the prophet to act out a living parable by caring for a flock doomed to slaughter. The people of Israel are pictured as helpless sheep whose corrupt ways are leading them toward ruin. This prophetic drama points forward to the Messiah as the Good Shepherd, sent to shepherd a nation heading into judgment.

The corrupt leaders of the nation act like greedy merchants who buy and sell sheep without any mercy. They slaughter the people spiritually and financially, feeling no guilt at all. Worst of all, they piously praise God for blessing them while getting rich off the misery of their own flock.

Because the nation has refused to repent, the Lord declares that His tender pity has reached its end. He will hand the people over to bitter internal conflict and the harsh rule of a foreign king. Without God's intervention, their land will be crushed and left without any deliverer.

The prophet carries out God's command and tends the flock, showing special care for the poor and afflicted who are willing to listen. He takes two shepherd's staffs, naming one Favor to show God's grace and protective care, and the other Union to represent brotherly harmony among the tribes. Together, these staffs picture God's ideal rule over a peaceful, united nation.

differ.view: The two staffs represent the preaching of the Gospel and the church ordinances that bind believers together.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The two staffs represent two ways God deals with people: gentle mercy through kindness, and discipline or punishment when they stray.

notes.meaning: In a very short time, the Good Shepherd removes three corrupt leaders who were misleading the flock. Yet despite His diligent care, the shepherd grows weary of their stubborn rebellion, and the people openly despise Him in return. Their mutual relationship breaks down because the flock will not accept His loving leadership.

differ.view: The three shepherds stand for the three offices of prophet, priest, and king, which were permanently dissolved when Israel rejected Jesus.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The three shepherds may refer to three wicked kings in Jeremiah's day or three corrupt high priests deposed in quick succession.

notes.meaning: Having been rejected, the shepherd steps down and refuses to pasture the ungrateful flock any longer. He leaves them to the natural consequences of their own rebellion, including famine, plague, and foreign invasion. Stripped of divine guidance, the people fall into fierce civil fighting and consume one another.

The shepherd snaps the staff named Favor in two to show that God is withdrawing His special protection. The agreement God made to hold back surrounding nations from crushing Israel is now cancelled. Without this shield of divine mercy, the nation is left wide open to destruction by foreign empires.

When the staff is broken on that day, the humble believers who had watched the shepherd understand what it means. While the wealthy and powerful leaders remain blind, this faithful remnant recognizes that the Lord's prophetic word is coming to pass. True faith often belongs to the lowly who take God's warnings to heart.

The shepherd asks the rulers to pay him whatever wages they think his hard labor was worth. In response, they insult him by weighing out thirty pieces of silver, the lowest compensation required by law for an injured slave. This contemptuous payout foreshadows how the chief priests would later value Jesus when paying Judas to betray Him.

The Lord speaks with bitter irony, mocking the petty sum as a grand price placed on His own divine ministry. He tells Zechariah to cast the silver to the potter, and the prophet hurls the money into the house of the Lord. This act directly anticipates Judas tossing his blood money back into the temple, which was then used to buy a potter's field.

Breaking the second staff, named Union, signals the total collapse of brotherly peace among the people. The unity between the tribes of Judah and Israel is destroyed, giving way to bitter division and civil strife. This inner crumbling helped pave the way for the nation's final defeat and scattering.

The Lord commands the prophet to take up the gear of a foolish shepherd and act out a new role. In Scripture, a fool is someone who is morally corrupt and acts against God's wisdom. Because the people rejected the Good Shepherd, they are warned that they will fall under the rule of cruel leaders who exploit them.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this foolish shepherd specifically pictures the coming Antichrist, who will arise during the end times to deceive and oppress Israel.

notes.meaning: This false shepherd does the exact opposite of what a caring guide should do. He ignores the lost, refuses to tend the wounded, and neglects the weary, caring only about his own greed. He feeds on the best sheep and violently tears them apart, painting a dark picture of ruthless and selfish rulers.

differ.view: This foolish shepherd points ultimately to the future Antichrist, who will deceive the Jewish people and then treat them with great cruelty.

notes.meaning: God pronounces a curse of doom on the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock in their time of need. A sword of judgment falls on his strong arm and his right eye, which stand for his power and insight. The ruler who abused his strength will find his power withered and his understanding completely blinded.
